Clinical Artificial Intelligence Faces Accountability Gaps Across Healthcare Lifecycles Study Reports

Artificial intelligence technologies increasingly support medical diagnosis, treatment planning, therapeutic drug dosing, triage, and population health surveillance, yet the structural frameworks governing algorithmic failure remain fragmented across international healthcare systems. Writing in Frontiers in Digital Health, Emmanuel Kumah of the University of Education, Winneba, and Eunice Agyei of Komfo Anokye Teaching Hospital examine what they define as an accountability vacuum in clinical medicine. The researchers clarify that this term does not denote an absolute legal void where applicable law is absent, but rather describes a pervasive operational gap in the assignment and practical execution of responsibilities across the artificial intelligence lifecycle. As machine learning models and deep neural networks become deeply embedded in point-of-care decisions, existing medico-legal doctrines struggle to address a fundamental question: when an algorithm errs, accountability remains divided unpredictably among the treating clinician who relied on the output, the healthcare institution that procured and deployed the software, and the commercial developer who trained the underlying computational model.

To demonstrate that accountability gaps stem from systemic implementation failures rather than abstract ethical dilemmas, the authors examine four documented cases where artificial intelligence diverged sharply from developer promises. The first prominent failure involves IBM Watson for Oncology, which was marketed to cancer hospitals internationally as an automated clinical decision-support tool. In 2018, investigative reporting by STAT News revealed internal company documents detailing multiple instances of unsafe and erroneous treatment recommendations produced by the system. Although Memorial Sloan Kettering disputed assertions that dangerous advice reached actual patients—clarifying that the cited errors occurred during rigorous software testing environments—the episode underscores how unrepresentative training datasets and inadequate pre-deployment verification can compromise system safety long before an algorithm interacts with patients in routine clinical workflows.

A second documented case reveals the severe risks of uncritical commercial deployment without rigorous local validation, exemplified by the Epic Sepsis Model implemented across hundreds of hospitals in the United States. When researchers conducted an independent evaluation of the proprietary predictive algorithm across 38,455 hospitalizations at a major academic medical center, its real-world discrimination dropped substantially below vendor claims. The independent team observed an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of only 0.63, contrasting sharply with previously reported developer estimates ranging from 0.76 to 0.83. At the standard alert threshold utilized in clinical practice, the model failed to identify 67 percent of patients suffering from sepsis, yet simultaneously generated automated warning alerts for 18 percent of all hospitalized patients. Kumah and Agyei argue that this failure underscores an unresolved jurisdictional dilemma regarding whether commercial software vendors or resource-strained healthcare institutions bear primary operational responsibility for validating predictive performance in localized clinical environments.

Operational vulnerabilities also emerge when advanced algorithms confront real-world clinical infrastructure, as documented during a human-centered evaluation of a deep learning screening system for diabetic retinopathy across eleven clinics in Thailand. During the first six months of implementation, 393 of 1,838 processed retinal images—representing fully 21 percent of all submitted photographs—failed to satisfy the algorithm’s automated image-quality standards. The high failure rate was driven by environmental and physical factors rather than algorithmic code, including non-darkened examination rooms, a specialized fundus camera requiring technical repair, and inconsistent administration of pupil-dilating eye drops across local facilities. The authors pair this technical mismatch with a fourth case illustrating algorithmic bias, where a commercial risk-prediction tool widely used by United States health systems systematically underestimated the complex health needs of Black patients.

Analyzing the structural dimensions of this accountability vacuum, Kumah and Agyei identify significant hurdles in applying conventional legal and clinical doctrines to software-related patient injuries. Citing foundational analyses by Mello and Guha, the perspective highlights that judicial systems encounter profound uncertainty when determining fault for injuries involving computational tools, largely because traditional product-liability doctrines historically applied to tangible physical goods rather than intangible software code. Allocating singular responsibility to clinicians who accept algorithmically generated guidance is ethically problematic when the software functions as an uninterpretable black box, yet insulating clinicians entirely overlooks the necessity of independent professional judgement. Furthermore, post-deployment surveillance remains severely neglected; the authors cite qualitative research by Owens and colleagues across 21 healthcare experts who identified an ongoing post-marketing responsibility vacuum.

The second and third structural dimensions center on algorithmic opacity and the institutionalization of health disparities. Drawing on analyses by Chustecki, the authors emphasize that deep learning models present interpretability challenges that complicate the doctrine of informed consent. Kumah and Agyei argue against unworkable mandates requiring disclosure of complete source code, advocating instead for risk-proportionate explainability tailored to specific audiences. Clinicians require clear descriptions of intended use, known contraindications, uncertainty metrics, and explicit criteria for overriding recommendations, while patients require clear notice when algorithms materially inform their care. Addressing algorithmic bias, the authors cite Alowais and colleagues to show that training models on historical datasets deficient in women, racial minorities, and elderly individuals inevitably embeds clinical disparities. Kumah and Agyei stress that while biased outputs do not automatically establish legal liability, healthcare institutions must actively monitor subgroup performance and maintain audited corrective protocols.

Regulatory frameworks across international jurisdictions have begun addressing these systemic risks, though current statutory mechanisms remain uneven. Reviewing policies as of the paper’s November 1, 2026 cutoff date, the authors examine the European Union’s regulatory landscape, where the AI Act under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 classifies medical device algorithms as high-risk technologies subject to mandatory risk management, technical documentation, and conformity assessments. However, the subsequent Digital Omnibus on AI under Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 deferred the operational enforcement of Annex I high-risk requirements until August 2, 2028. Meanwhile, the revised European Union Product Liability Directive 2024/2853 explicitly expands product definitions to encompass software and artificial intelligence placed on the market after December 8, 2026, though the European Commission withdrew its proposed AI Liability Directive in October 2025. Across the Atlantic, the United States Food and Drug Administration finalized guidance in August 2025 governing predetermined change control plans for machine learning devices, while its comprehensive lifecycle management framework remained a draft as of January 2025.
